Rendered with the same ambiguity, not corrected.

titre: The Donation of Constantine: The Forgery That Latin Betrayed (Valla, 1440)
accroche: A humanist rereads the title on which the temporal power of the popes rested, and catches it out on a single word: “satraps.”
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 1440, in Naples, a humanist in the service of the King of Aragon rereads a text that the Church had invoked for centuries: the Donation of Constantine. According to this document, the emperor Constantine, cured of leprosy by Pope Sylvester, ceded to the bishop of Rome the Lateran palace, the imperial insignia, and authority over the West. Lorenzo Valla does not try to find out whether the scene is plausible. He reads the Latin.

## A Forgery Unmasked by Grammar

Valla worked in 1439-1440 for Alfonso V of Aragon, then in a territorial conflict with Pope Eugene IV. His treatise, the *De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione declamatio* (Discourse on the Forgery of the Alleged Donation of Constantine), is not content with objections of common sense. It picks out the text's anachronisms, one by one. The document mentions “satraps” sitting in Roman councils: Valla asks who has ever heard of satraps in the councils of the Romans, the word belonging to another world. He notes that the decree speaks of Constantinople as an already established patriarchal see, when it claims to be dated a few days after Constantine's baptism, long before the city existed under that name. He finally mocks the Roman clergy being promoted to “patricians and consuls,” titles one does not become by a simple decree and that an emperor would not have entrusted to clerics. And he judges the Latin of the text too heavy and too stilted to have come out of the imperial chancery of the 4th century.

Historians today date the forgery to the 8th century, around the middle of it, or even to the 9th: a first version may have served Pope Stephen II in his negotiations with Pepin the Short, around 754.

## What This Shifts

It is often said that Valla killed the Donation with a stroke of the pen. The story is less clear-cut. The text had already been challenged, as early as the year 1001 according to specialists, and Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa held it to be apocryphal before Valla. And Valla's demonstration, written for a king who had his reasons to harm the pope, remained in manuscript for a long time: it was not printed until 1517, by Ulrich von Hutten, just as Luther was shaking the Church. Nor did it carry conviction all at once: it was the historian Cesare Baronio who, in his *Annales ecclésiastiques* (Ecclesiastical Annals), published between 1588 and 1607, sealed the verdict of a forgery almost unanimously accepted.

What remains is the method: a text can be dated by its vocabulary, without knowing anything about the politics of its time. A philologist's proof took more than a century to win out, and it did not need its author's enthusiasm to do so. What remains to be seen is which other texts that we take to be ancient are held up only by the fact that no one has reread their Latin.

repere.texte: Valla composes his treatise in 1439-1440 for Alfonso V of Aragon. The text of the forgery is judged to date from the 8th century, it is published for the first time in 1517 by Ulrich von Hutten, some seventy years later, and the verdict becomes almost unanimous only with Baronio's Annals (1588-1607).
repere.source: Valla, De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione (Discourse on the Forgery of the Alleged Donation of Constantine), 1440 (trans. Coleman, 1922); Wikipedia, Donation of Constantine

carte.punch: An 8th-century forgery unmasked in 1440 by the vocabulary of its Latin.
carte.idee: In 1440, Lorenzo Valla shows that the Donation of Constantine is a forgery: the text speaks of “satraps” and of a patriarchal see at Constantinople before the city existed under that name. But his treatise is not printed until 1517, and the verdict becomes almost unanimous only with Baronio (1588-1607).

quiz.question: What kind of evidence does Valla's demonstration against the Donation mainly rest on?
choix: The text itself: vocabulary and Latin impossible in the 4th century, such as “satraps” or Constantinople
An authentic manuscript of Constantine found in the Vatican archives
The confession of a copyist who admits having fabricated the document for the pope
A chemical analysis of the ink and parchment of the original document
quiz.explication: Valla has neither an archive nor a confession: he reads the text and finds in it words and titles from another time. Ink analysis did not exist, no authentic manuscript of Constantine is invoked, and no copyist confessed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When is Valla's treatise first printed?
choix: In 1440, right after it was written
In 1001, under the emperor Otto III
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1439-1440 treatise remains in manuscript until 1517, when Ulrich von Hutten prints it. Baronio, for his part, writes at the end of the 16th century, and the year 1001 is the date of the first challenge to the Donation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who employed Valla when he wrote against the Donation?
choix: Alfonso V of Aragon, in conflict with the Papal States
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Valla worked for Alfonso V of Aragon, in a territorial dispute with Pope Eugene IV. Luther praised Valla only later, and Nicholas of Cusa, a cardinal, had also cast doubt on the Donation.
